issues.description: Silent semantic change from req.stream.read() to req.bounded_stream.read() smuggled into example
issues.detail: The change in examples/things_advanced.py replaces req.stream.read() with req.bounded_stream.read(). These are not equivalent: bounded_stream is bounded by Content-Length and will read exactly that many bytes (or block/return empty if the header lies), whereas req.stream may be the raw WSGI input. The PR description claims the change is to 'add req.content_length to req.stream.read()' — which is not what the diff does. The author has not stated the precondition (what Content-Length values are admissible), the postcondition (what body contains when Content-Length is a lie), or why bounded_stream is correct here. This is UNREASONED.

issues.description: FAQ example demonstrates the wrong discipline: it tests an unreasoned handler
issues.detail: The PostTest handler in the FAQ reads req.stream.read(req.content_length or 0) and treats Content-Length=1 with an empty body as a 400. There is no stated invariant for what the handler guarantees when the client lies about Content-Length. The handler conflates 'client sent declared bytes that decoded to falsy' with 'client lied'. A reader cannot derive the postcondition from the code. This is the kind of folklore-by-example that propagates UNREASONED patterns into user code; the FAQ should either prove the property or not advertise it.

issues.description: Test asserts status code without asserting the failure mode that justified the test
issues.detail: resp4 in tests/test_examples.py sends Content-Length: 1 with an empty body and asserts status_code == 400. But the example handler raises HTTPBadRequest for 'Empty request body' on `if not body:` — which is the same 400 that an honest empty POST would produce. The test does not distinguish 'bounded_stream returned empty because body was empty' from 'bounded_stream blocked, raised, or returned partial data due to the Content-Length lie'. The postcondition the test claims to verify (correct handling of mismatched Content-Length) is not actually verified by the assertion. TESTED-NOT-PROVED.

issues.description: PR description does not match the diff
issues.detail: The summary says: 'Update things_advanced.py example to add req.content_length to req.stream.read()'. The actual change replaces req.stream with req.bounded_stream and passes no argument. Either the author did not understand the change they made, or the description was not updated. Either failure mode indicates the change was not reasoned about before being written.

issues.description: README.rst diff is a sprawling reformat unrelated to the stated purpose of the PR
issues.detail: The PR title and description scope is: add POST request tests for the things_advanced example, plus an FAQ entry. The README diff reformats argument lists, changes string concatenation to .format(), changes resp.status construction, alters StorageError.handle signature, and switches req.stream to req.bounded_stream in inline example code. These are not in the stated frame. Mixing a behavioral change (bounded_stream) with cosmetic reflow in the same patch makes the patch harder to reason about and review. Separate the concerns.

issues.description: StorageError.handle signature change in README is a silent API contract change
issues.detail: The README inline example changes StorageError.handle(ex, req, resp, params) to handle(req, resp, ex, params). If this reflects the actual framework convention, fine — but it is presented without explanation in a PR scoped to test additions. A reader cannot tell from this patch whether the README was wrong before, or is wrong now. State the invariant; do not silently mutate it.

issues.description: FAQ test code uses non-idiomatic and slightly wrong Python
issues.detail: The FAQ example uses `assert(result.status == falcon.HTTP_400)` (parenthesized assert — looks like a function call but is not), and constructs headers as a list of tuples `[('Content-Length', '1'),]` when the rest of the codebase uses dicts. Trailing comma inside a single-element list is harmless but the parenthesized assert is a known Python antipattern (PEP 8, and `assert(x, y)` would silently always pass). Documentation examples should model the discipline the framework expects of its users.

issues.description: No news fragment visible in the diff despite checklist claim
issues.detail: The checklist asserts that towncrier news fragments under docs/_newsfragments/ have been added. The diff shows no such file. Either the checklist is incorrect, or the fragment was added but is not in the diff shown. The discipline of the checklist depends on it being true; ticked-but-not-done is worse than not ticked.

review.summary: The PR claims a narrow scope — POST tests and an FAQ entry — but smuggles a behavioral change (req.stream -> req.bounded_stream) into the example and the README, and the description even misstates what that change does. None of the new artifacts (the example change, the FAQ handler, the resp4 assertion) state a precondition for what happens when the client lies about Content-Length, and the test that purports to verify the mismatched-Content-Length case asserts only a status code that the honest-empty-body path also returns — TESTED-NOT-PROVED. The FAQ example additionally propagates a parenthesized `assert(...)` antipattern into user-facing docs. The tests as written do increase coverage of the happy POST path, which has value, but the interesting case is not actually pinned down. Verdict: UNREASONED; would require the author to state the spec of bounded_stream vs stream in this handler, and to assert a property that distinguishes the lie-about-Content-Length path from the empty-body path, before this should land.
